authoredPrompt: This figure illustrates a Gouy balance apparatus used to measure magnetic susceptibility, showing a vertically suspended sample tube positioned between two cylindrical electromagnets and counterbalanced on a traditional beam balance against calibrated reference weights. The sample tube, labeled "Sample," hangs from one arm of the balance beam down into the gap between the two poles labeled "Electromagnets," while the opposite arm holds a pan carrying calibrated masses; the label "Magnetic field" with a line points to the region inside the gap, where curved purple arrows radiate outward in concentric arcs representing the inhomogeneous field lines diverging from the magnet poles. Because a paramagnetic sample containing unpaired electrons is drawn into the stronger-field region of the gap, it experiences a net downward force that makes it appear heavier, shifting the beam, while a diamagnetic sample with all electrons paired is weakly repelled and appears slightly lighter. The change in apparent mass — measured by adding or removing calibrated weights until the beam re-levels — is proportional to the number of unpaired electrons in the sample, providing a direct experimental count of those electrons. This figure introduces the Gouy balance as the key instrument for determining magnetic susceptibility and motivates its use to reveal that O2 possesses two unpaired electrons, a fact the Lewis-structure model fails to predict.
authoredInteractions:
- Toggle between a paramagnetic sample and a diamagnetic sample: watch the balance tip toward the magnet or away from it and update the sign of the magnetic susceptibility
- Slider for magnetic field strength: observe proportional deflection of the balance arm and read off the corresponding susceptibility value
- Animate the weighing procedure: show the sample tube being drawn into or repelled from the magnetic field region as the electromagnets energize
authoredContext:
Magnetic susceptibility measures the force experienced by a substance in a magnetic field. When we compare the weight of a sample to the weight measured in a magnetic field ( ), paramagnetic samples that are attracted to the magnet will appear heavier because of the force exerted by the magnetic field. We can calculate the number of unpaired electrons based on the increase in weight.

A Gouy balance compares the mass of a sample in the presence of a magnetic field with the mass with the electromagnet turned off to determine the number of unpaired electrons in a sample.

A diagram depicts a stand supporting two objects that are held in balance by a horizontal bar. On the right, the bar supports a dish that is holding two weights. On the left there is a line attached to a test tube labeled, “Sample tube.” The test tube has been lowered into the space labeled, “Magnetic field,” between two structures labeled, “Electromagnets.”

Experiments show that each O 2 molecule has two unpaired electrons. The Lewis-structure model does not predict the presence of these two unpaired electrons. Unlike oxygen, the apparent weight of most molecules decreases slightly in the presence of an inhomogeneous magnetic field. Materials in which all of the electrons are paired are diamagnetic and weakly repel a magnetic field. Paramagnetic and diamagnetic materials do not act as permanent magnets. Only in the presence of an applied magnetic field do they demonstrate attraction or repulsion.

discrepancies: Sample tube hangs far to the left, completely outside the gap between the electromagnets, instead of passing down through the magnetic field gap as in the source
Blue liquid inside the sample tube is not visible — the tube appears as an empty grey/white cylinder
Electromagnets are rendered dark near-black instead of the silver-grey metallic cylinders in the source
Magnetic field lines are sparse and faint (a few horizontal lines and loops) versus the dense purple dipole pattern with many arrowheads in the source
Beam is noticeably tilted and the tube angled, whereas the source shows a level beam with a vertical hanging tube
evaluation.notes: All major components (gold balance, pan with weights, tube, electromagnets, field lines, labels) and meaningful interactions are present, but the sample tube is misplaced outside the magnet gap and the blue liquid is invisible, undermining the core Gouy-balance arrangement.
action_items: Reposition the sample tube (or move the electromagnets left) so the lower part of the tube sits in the gap between the two pole faces, matching the source
Make the blue liquid clearly visible inside the glass tube (raise opacity, ensure correct render order)
Change the electromagnet material from dark to silver-grey metallic to match the source
Add more purple field-line curves with arrowheads to reproduce the dense dipole field pattern of the source
